passage:
Playground duty, week before Diwali: note for the Class 5 file.
During the rangoli break, Tanvir pushed Bidisha off the bench and she scraped her elbow on the stones. I took her to the first-aid room myself; it was a small scrape, but she was shaking.
When I sat down with Tanvir, he folded his arms. "She was annoying. She kept saying our rangoli was crooked. She asked for it."
I asked, "What did Bidisha do with her hands?"
"Nothing. She just talked."
"And what did you do with yours?"
He was quiet, then said, "Pushed."
Next steps: Tanvir will apologise tomorrow and help redraw the rangoli with Bidisha's team, and I phoned both families this evening.

qa.q: What happened to Bidisha's elbow?
qa.a: She scraped it on the stones when Tanvir pushed her off the bench.

qa.q: Why does "She asked for it" feel true to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir felt angry and irritated about the crooked-rangoli comments, and blaming Bidisha lets him feel justified instead of guilty about the push.

qa.q: How did the adult's questions help Tanvir?
qa.a: Asking what each child did with their hands separated talking from pushing, so Tanvir named his own action; an apology, a repair job and calls home followed.

qa.q: What was the break like for Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha was pushed, scraped her elbow and was shaking, so it was frightening and painful for her, whatever she had said about the rangoli.

grounding: A child says the classmate he pushed was annoying and deserved it, turning the victim into the cause.

subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage:
Hi Mitali di,
Exams are done, finally. Weird week though. You remember Vidya from my building? In class, the boys at the back have started calling her "Siren" because her voice goes high when she answers. Every time she speaks, someone makes a siren noise. Yesterday she stopped answering at all, even when Ma'am asked her directly.
Honestly, she needs to toughen up. Everyone gets called something. If she just laughed along, they'd get bored. I told her that at the bus stop, and she looked at me like I'd slapped her. Then she walked the long way home alone.
When Ma'am asked me after class whether something was going on with Vidya, I said I didn't know.
It's easier when people don't make such a big deal, right? Anyway, I'm fine. Write back about college.
Sonali

qa.q: What do the boys at the back call Vidya?
qa.a: "Siren".

qa.q: Why might it feel easier for Sonali to say Vidya should toughen up?
qa.a: Sonali seems uncomfortable watching the teasing; making Vidya responsible spares Sonali the awkward, scary job of standing up to the boys, and "I'm fine" hints at unease underneath.

qa.q: What could Sonali do instead?
qa.a: Sonali could tell Vidya the teasing isn't her fault, refuse to laugh along, and tell Ma'am honestly what has been happening, today rather than later.

qa.q: How did Sonali's advice land for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya looked as if she had been slapped and walked home alone, so it probably felt like a friend taking the bullies' side.

grounding: A teenager watching a friend being teased says she should toughen up, making the target responsible to avoid discomfort.

subtype: Being told it was own fault [Receiver]
passage:
Chhath was two days away, and the whole courtyard in Begusarai smelled of thekua frying, when Pooja finally said it: she had paid four thousand rupees as a "processing fee" on a scholarship call that turned out to be fake. The number was switched off now.
Her uncle put down his tea. "An educated girl, falling for this? You should have been smarter." Pooja stared at the floor and went inside.
Preeti found her on the roof, knees pulled up, and sat beside her without a lecture. "Tell me exactly what happened." She listened to all of it. Then: "They're the ones who lied. They do this to hundreds of people."
Together they wrote down the date, the number and the payment details, called the bank's helpline, and filed a report with the cyber crime helpline before dark. Pooja's shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What had Pooja paid four thousand rupees for?
qa.a: A "processing fee" on a scholarship call that turned out to be fake.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling after her uncle's words?
qa.a: Pooja felt ashamed and small, staring at the floor and going inside, because the blame piled shame on top of the loss.

qa.q: What made Preeti's help work?
qa.a: Preeti listened without lecturing, said the scammers were the ones who lied, and then took practical steps the same day: writing the details down, calling the bank helpline and filing a report.

qa.q: How might the uncle see his own comment, and what does it miss?
qa.a: The uncle may think he is being practical or teaching a lesson, but it misses that the scammers chose to deceive, and the blame only made Pooja retreat.

grounding: A young woman cheated in a scam is told she should have been smarter, and supportive listening plus practical steps help her recover.

passage:
In the office canteen in Salt Lake, Salma told Arnab that Rituparna from her team had finally reported the senior manager who had been shouting at her in meetings for four months, calling her "useless" in front of clients.
"Four months?" Arnab said. "Why did she let it go on so long? She should have—" He stopped, spoon halfway to his mouth.
"Should have what?" Salma asked.
Arnab put the spoon down. "No. Wrong question. Who was doing the shouting? He was. Every meeting, he chose to. She was the one trying to keep her job."
Salma nodded slowly. "That's what the HR head said too. They're looking into his conduct, not hers."
"Tell her I said she did a hard thing," Arnab said. "And that none of it was on her."

qa.q: How long had the senior manager been shouting at Rituparna?
qa.a: For four months.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he stopped with the spoon halfway?
qa.a: Arnab seemed to feel a jolt of discomfort, even embarrassment, catching himself blaming Rituparna the moment the words came out.

qa.q: Why is "Who was doing the shouting?" a better question?
qa.a: It puts responsibility back on the person who chose to cause harm, instead of asking the target to explain why she put up with it.

qa.q: How might Rituparna feel hearing Arnab's message?
qa.a: Rituparna would likely feel relieved and supported, hearing that reporting was a hard thing done well and that the shouting was never her fault. 🤍

grounding: An adult catches himself asking why a target let harm go on and asks instead who acted and what they chose.

subtype: At least it was not worse [Actor]
passage:
The mangoes were ripening in Payal's village near Ratnagiri, and summer holidays meant cricket every afternoon in the lane behind the post office. Payal's big hit went straight through the postmaster's side window. Glass on the sill, a crack running across the pane.
Jaya gasped. Payal shrugged, fast. "It's only one small window. Last year the big boys broke the whole school gate and smashed two bulbs. That was bad. This is nothing."
"The postmaster will be angry," Jaya said.
"He should be angry with them, not me. Mine was an accident, and it's tiny compared to theirs." Payal picked up the ball and walked on, but she didn't hit another six that day, and she kept glancing back at the crack.

qa.q: Whose window did Payal's hit break?
qa.a: The postmaster's side window.

qa.q: Why does comparing with the big boys make Payal feel better?
qa.a: Next to a broken gate and two bulbs, one crack feels tiny, so Payal can push away the guilt; still, glancing back at the crack suggests she feels uneasy.

qa.q: What could Payal do instead of comparing?
qa.a: Payal could knock on the postmaster's door, say it was an accident and she is sorry, and ask a grown-up at home to help set it right.

qa.q: How might the postmaster see it?
qa.a: To the postmaster, a cracked window is still a cracked window, whatever the big boys did last year, and walking away would likely bother him more than the accident.

grounding: A child who broke a window says it is nothing compared with what older boys did, making her own wrong look small.

subtype: Cutting corners because the rest do worse [Actor]
passage:
On Uttarayan the whole of Anand was up on the terraces, kites everywhere, and Payal sat on the stairs of the girls' hostel transferring fifteen hundred rupees to a senior who "did assignments". Her sociology project was due Monday.
Minakshi came down with a spool of kite string. "Is that the ghost-writer guy?"
"Don't look at me like that. Do you know how many people in this town have bought their whole degree? The chemist's son has a certificate from a college he never even saw. Compared to that, one project is nothing."
"I'm not talking about him. I'm talking about you. You argued with Sir for an hour about plagiarism last term."
Payal locked the phone and looked up at the kites. "That was different," she said, but she didn't sound sure.

qa.q: Who was Payal sending fifteen hundred rupees to?
qa.a: A senior who "did assignments".

qa.q: Why does "others buy whole degrees" make Payal feel better?
qa.a: Measured against the worst example, one bought project looks tiny, so Payal can quiet her guilt; not sounding sure shows the unease is still there.

qa.q: What could pull Payal back to her own standard?
qa.a: Judging it by what Payal herself argued about plagiarism last term, not by the chemist's son; she could ask Sir for more time instead of buying the project.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel watching this?
qa.a: Minakshi seems disappointed and uneasy, remembering how strongly Payal once argued against plagiarism.

grounding: A student paying for a ghostwritten project says others buy whole degrees, setting the bar by the worst example instead of her own values.

passage:
It was 11:50 pm, ten minutes before the finance portal closed for the month, and the hotel Wi-Fi kept dropping. Kishore's expense claim for the Nagpur trip was short: two lunches had no receipts. His teammate had said everyone just adds a "client dinner" to round it off.
He typed the line: Client dinner, ₹1,800. The cursor blinked.
He thought of Irawati, three years old and asleep at home, and pictured her reading this line one day. Then he pictured Deshpande, the colleague he trusted most, looking over his shoulder.
Would he be comfortable?
No.
He deleted it, submitted the claim as it was, and wrote to finance: "Two meals without receipts. Can I add them with a written declaration?" The portal closed at 11:59. He shut the laptop, feeling oddly light.

qa.q: What line did Kishore type and then delete?
qa.a: "Client dinner, ₹1,800."

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after deleting the line?
qa.a: Kishore felt oddly light, relieved to have acted by his own standard even though the claim stayed short.

qa.q: What made Kishore's test effective under time pressure?
qa.a: Picturing Irawati and Deshpande reading the line gave a quick personal standard instead of "everyone does it", and the note to finance gave an honest route for the missing receipts.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had followed his teammate's advice?
qa.a: The claim would look complete, but a fake dinner would sit in the records for Kishore to keep defending, and the next shortcut would feel smaller.

grounding: An adult tempted to add a fake expense asks whether he would be comfortable if his child or most trusted colleague saw it, and does not.

passage:
Class 3 Christmas party, 20 December: note.
A glass bauble Thomas had brought from home fell and broke. I was at the door. Asif, standing nearest, said at once, "The fan blew it off." The fan was off.
By lunch he was telling it with new details: the bauble "wobbled first", he "tried to catch it". At home time he told his mother, completely sure and a little hurt, "I saw the fan do it, I was right there." He no longer seemed to be lying; he seemed to believe it.
I did not call him a liar. Tomorrow I will sit with him, say accidents happen and I am not angry, and ask for the very first thing he remembers. Thomas still needs a proper sorry.

qa.q: What did Asif say right after the bauble broke?
qa.a: "The fan blew it off."

qa.q: Why might Asif now feel so sure the fan did it?
qa.a: Each retelling added details until the story felt like a memory; believing it keeps Asif safe from trouble and shame, so he even feels a little hurt at being doubted.

qa.q: How does the teacher plan to help Asif?
qa.a: By not calling him a liar, making the truth safe to tell ("accidents happen, I'm not angry"), and asking for the very first thing he remembers before the story grows further.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel about the broken bauble?
qa.a: Thomas brought it from home, so Thomas is probably sad about losing it and may feel let down if nobody owns up.

grounding: A teacher notices a child's fib to avoid trouble turning, with each retelling, into a version he believes.

passage:
Snow closed the schools in Ankara for two days before the biology test, and Elif spent them on the sofa flipping through her notes with a mug of salep. Every page looked familiar: the cell diagrams, the coloured headings, even the coffee stain on page four. "I know this," she told Selin on the phone. "I've read it three times."
Selin was writing answers to old questions without looking at anything. "Try explaining osmosis to me without the notes."
"I don't need to. I'll recognise it on the paper."
On Monday there was no diagram. The paper asked her to explain, in her own words, why a slice of potato goes soft in salt water. Elif's pen hovered. The page she could picture perfectly would not turn into sentences. When the results came back she stared at the mark and whispered, "But I read it three times."

qa.q: How many times did Elif say she had read the notes?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Elif feel so sure she knew the material?
qa.a: Every page looked familiar, and that easy recognition felt like knowing, so Elif felt confident, and then shocked when she had to explain in her own words.

qa.q: What study habit could fix this?
qa.a: Testing herself the way Selin did: closing the notes and explaining ideas like osmosis aloud or answering old questions, which shows what she actually understands.

qa.q: How might Selin see Elif's way of studying?
qa.a: Selin seems a little worried that Elif is too confident, which is why Selin suggests explaining osmosis without the notes. 🤔

grounding: A teenager who re-read her notes feels sure she knows the topic and is shocked by the result, mistaking familiarity for understanding.
